Home Loan vs Renting: What the Real Numbers Say in 2026

Published: 17 January 2026 · Updated: 15 May 2026 · By Priya Sharma, CFA

"Renting is throwing money away." You have heard it at family dinners, from bank advertisements, and probably from that one colleague who bought a house and hasn't stopped talking about it since. But in 2026, with Australian variable mortgage rates sitting above 6% and Indian home loan rates starting at 7.10% p.a., the maths behind this claim deserves a closer look — with actual numbers, not slogans.

This article breaks down the true annual cost of owning versus renting in both Australia and India, using real 2026 rate data, and explains when each option genuinely makes financial sense.

The Hidden Costs of Buying a Home

Most people compare a mortgage repayment to a rent payment and declare buying the winner. That comparison misses roughly half the costs of ownership.

Australia: What It Really Costs to Own in 2026

In May 2026, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised the cash rate by 0.25%, bringing it to 4.35%. All major lenders — ANZ, NAB, CBA, and Westpac — passed on the full increase effective 15 May 2026. Variable home loan rates now sit broadly in the 6.2%–6.8% range depending on the lender and your loan-to-value ratio.

Take a median Sydney house priced at A$1,100,000 (CoreLogic median, 2026) purchased with a 20% deposit of A$220,000. Your loan is A$880,000 at 6.5% over 30 years. The monthly repayment is approximately A$5,561, or A$66,732 annually. But that is just where the costs begin.

Add council rates (approximately A$2,000/year), water rates (A$900), building and contents insurance (A$2,400), and maintenance — typically estimated at 1% of property value per year, so A$11,000 for a A$1.1M property. Your total annual holding cost comes to approximately A$83,032.

The same Sydney property rents for around A$950–A$1,050 per week in 2026. At A$1,000/week, that is A$52,000 per year. The annual cost of buying exceeds the annual cost of renting by roughly A$31,000 in year one.

There is also the opportunity cost of your deposit. If your A$220,000 down payment were invested in a diversified ASX index fund returning 8% per annum, it would generate A$17,600 in year one alone. This is real money you forgo by tying capital up in a property.

India: What It Really Costs to Own in 2026

In India, the RBI repo rate stands at 5.25% as of April 2026, with most floating-rate home loans benchmarked to the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR). Home loan rates from leading banks currently range from 7.50% to 8.70% p.a. from SBI, 7.75% p.a. from HDFC Bank, and 8.75%+ from ICICI Bank, depending on your credit score and borrower profile.

Consider a 2BHK flat in Bangalore worth ₹85 lakh, purchased with a 20% down payment of ₹17 lakh and a home loan of ₹68 lakh at 8.5% p.a. over 20 years. The EMI works out to approximately ₹59,100 per month, or ₹7.09 lakh annually. Over the 20-year tenure, you repay a total of ₹1.42 crore — meaning the interest alone costs ₹74 lakh on top of the ₹68 lakh principal.

Beyond the EMI, ownership adds stamp duty and registration (approximately 5–7% of property value in most states, so ₹4.25–5.95 lakh one-time), society maintenance charges (₹3,000–₹6,000 per month in a gated community), property tax (₹10,000–₹25,000 per year depending on the city), and home insurance. In year one, total ownership costs including the EMI can easily reach ₹9–10 lakh.

The equivalent 2BHK in Bangalore rents for approximately ₹25,000–₹35,000 per month (₹3–4.2 lakh per year). The annual gap between owning and renting costs is significant — often ₹5–6 lakh or more in the early years of the loan.

The True Cost of Renting

Rent is not without financial consequences. The financial case for renting entirely depends on what you do with the money you save by not owning.

If an Australian renter saves A$31,000 per year (the annual ownership premium in our Sydney example) and invests it systematically at 8% annual returns, that disciplined strategy builds substantial wealth. After 10 years, that annual investment compounds to over A$450,000. After 20 years, it could exceed A$1.5 million.

The equivalent logic applies in India. A renter saving ₹5–6 lakh annually and investing through SIPs in diversified mutual funds at a 12% historical CAGR would accumulate a significant corpus over the same 20-year period.

The word "could" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in both those sentences. The behavioural reality is that most renters do not invest the difference. They absorb lifestyle inflation, increase spending, or simply keep it in a low-interest savings account. The enforced savings discipline of a monthly mortgage repayment is one of homeownership's most underrated advantages — not because property is necessarily the best investment, but because it makes saving non-negotiable.

When Buying Wins: The Break-Even Calculation

Buying a home makes strong financial sense in specific circumstances, and the calculation comes down to three variables: how long you hold the property, the rate of capital growth, and the price-to-rent ratio in your market.

The Break-Even Holding Period

In high-priced Australian markets like Sydney and Melbourne, transaction costs alone consume a large portion of early equity gains. Stamp duty on a A$1.1M Sydney purchase is approximately A$46,000. Add conveyancing, building inspections, and agent commissions on eventual sale (typically 2–2.5% of sale price), and the break-even holding period before buying becomes financially superior to renting is generally 7–10 years in Sydney and Melbourne.

In more affordable markets — Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth, or regional centres — price-to-rent ratios are lower, transaction costs as a percentage of purchase price are lower, and break-even can occur in 4–6 years.

In India, break-even is similarly market-dependent. In metros like Mumbai and Delhi where property is priced at 30–35x annual rent, the financial advantage of buying takes a decade or more to materialise. In Tier-2 cities like Pune, Hyderabad, or Ahmedabad, price-to-rent ratios of 15–20x annual rent mean buying can reach break-even within 5–7 years, especially with the capital appreciation these cities have delivered in recent years.

When Buying Clearly Makes Sense

Buying makes strong financial sense when:

  • You plan to hold the property for at least 7–10 years in a major city
  • You have a 20% deposit ready — avoiding Lenders Mortgage Insurance in Australia (which can add 1–3% of the loan value) or keeping your India LTV below 80%
  • Your income is stable enough to comfortably service the debt under APRA's 3% serviceability buffer (Australia) or the bank's standard stress-test (India)
  • You are buying in a market with genuine long-term demand drivers — population growth, infrastructure investment, and constrained land supply

When Renting Makes Financial Sense

Renting is the rational choice when your time horizon in a location is under five years, since you simply cannot amortise the transaction costs of buying and selling across a short holding period. It is also the sensible option when property prices in your target market are significantly above long-term fair value relative to rents — a situation that existed across most Australian capital cities throughout 2022–2025.

Renting also offers genuine non-financial advantages worth pricing in: mobility for career opportunities, no maintenance liability, and the flexibility to upgrade or downsize without transaction costs. These are real benefits, not consolation prizes.

Tax Angles That Change the Calculation

Taxes alter the comparison meaningfully in both markets and should never be ignored.

Australia: Negative Gearing and Capital Gains Tax

For Australian investors (not owner-occupiers), negative gearing allows losses from an investment property — where rental income falls short of holding costs — to be deducted against other income, effectively providing a tax subsidy on the shortfall. This makes investment property more attractive for high-income earners on the 37% or 45% marginal tax rate. However, negative gearing only helps if the property is eventually sold at a capital gain — meaning it remains a long-term play.

Capital gains on property held for more than 12 months qualify for a 50% CGT discount. On a A$300,000 gain from an investment property, only A$150,000 is added to assessable income — a significant concession.

India: Section 24 and Section 80C Deductions

Indian home loan borrowers benefit from two important tax deductions under the old income tax regime. Under Section 24(b), you can deduct up to ₹2 lakh annually on interest paid on a home loan for a self-occupied property. Under Section 80C, principal repayment qualifies for deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh per year as part of the aggregate 80C limit. Combined, a borrower in the 30% tax slab can save up to ₹1.05 lakh in tax annually through these deductions — a meaningful offset to the interest cost.

Note that under the new tax regime (default from FY 2023–24 onwards), these deductions are not available. Borrowers need to evaluate whether the deductions under the old regime outweigh the lower slab rates under the new regime for their income level. The Psychological and Non-Financial Factors

No article on this topic is honest if it ignores the non-financial dimensions of homeownership.

Security and stability are real benefits. Owning a home means no landlord can ask you to vacate, redevelop the property, or raise your rent above market every 12 months. In Australia, where no-grounds evictions remain legal in several states and rental vacancy rates in major cities are still below 2%, this security premium has real monetary value that does not show up in rent vs buy calculators.

In India, the cultural and social significance of owning a home remains profound — for families, for marriages, and for the sense of permanence it confers. These are legitimate considerations, even if they resist quantification.

Homeownership also carries genuine stress. Owning a home means owning its problems. A cracked foundation, a failed water heater, a roof leak — these are your responsibility, your timeline, and your bill. Renters transfer that liability entirely to landlords.

FAQs: Home Loan vs Renting in 2026

  • Is it better to buy or rent in Australia in 2026?

    It depends heavily on your city, time horizon, and deposit size. In Sydney and Melbourne, the annual cost of owning currently exceeds renting by A$25,000–A$35,000 for median properties, meaning renting and investing the difference makes financial sense for people who will move within 7 years. In more affordable cities like Brisbane, Adelaide, or Perth, the gap is smaller and the break-even period is shorter.

  • Is it better to buy or rent in India in 2026?

    In Tier-1 metros like Mumbai and Delhi where price-to-rent ratios exceed 30x, renting and investing the difference in SIPs or mutual funds can outperform buying over a 10-year horizon. In Tier-2 cities with lower price-to-rent ratios and stronger appreciation, buying can reach break-even within 5–7 years. The decision is also influenced by home loan tax deductions under Section 24(b) and 80C, which reduce the effective interest cost for borrowers in the old tax regime.

  • What is the current home loan interest rate in Australia in 2026?

    Following RBA rate hikes in 2026, variable home loan rates sit in the 6.2%–6.8% range across major lenders. ANZ, NAB, CBA, and Westpac all passed on the full 0.25% May 2026 increase effective 15 May 2026. The RBA cash rate is currently 4.35%.

  • What is the current home loan interest rate in India in 2026?

    As of May 2026, home loan rates in India start from 7.10%–7.50% p.a. for eligible borrowers at public sector banks, with SBI ranging from 7.50%–8.70% p.a. and HDFC Bank from 7.75% p.a. The RBI repo rate is 5.25% (unchanged at the April 2026 MPC meeting), keeping floating-rate EMIs stable for now.

  • Does renting mean throwing money away?

    No. Rent pays for housing — a genuine service with real value. Mortgage interest also represents money that does not build equity; it goes directly to the bank. For the first 5–10 years of a 30-year mortgage, the large majority of each repayment is interest, not principal. The relevant question is not whether rent is "wasted" but whether buying provides better value per rupee or dollar over your specific time horizon.

  • How much deposit do I need to avoid Lenders Mortgage Insurance (LMI) in Australia?

    A 20% deposit on the purchase price keeps your loan-to-value ratio (LVR) at or below 80%, which is the threshold to avoid LMI. On a A$900,000 property, that means A$180,000 upfront. Borrowers with less than a 20% deposit will be required to pay LMI, which can add A$10,000–A$30,000 to the total cost of the loan.

The Bottom Line

The real numbers in 2026 tell a nuanced story. Buying is not always better than renting, and renting is not always better than buying. The answer depends on your city, your time horizon, the size of your deposit, what you would do with the money if you didn't buy, and whether you have the discipline to invest the savings that renting can generate.

What the numbers do confirm is this: the true annual cost of homeownership is substantially higher than the monthly repayment figure suggests, and the case for buying is strongest for people who plan to stay put for the long term in markets with strong demand fundamentals and reasonable price-to-rent ratios.

Before making the biggest financial decision of your life, run the numbers for your specific situation.
